source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 1 core evidence. With test-execution feedback, repair at equal sample budget beats plain resampling only some of the time. Gains depend on spending budget on diverse first drafts, not on many repairs.
numbers: GPT-4 on APPS: 10 drafts + 1 repair each (up to 20 samples) = 1.05x the pass@20 baseline; 2 drafts + 10 repairs each (up to 22) = 0.97x pass@22. Best case GPT-4 +8% relative on APPS; GPT-3.5 only marginal; Code Llama up to +10% on HumanEval; GPT-3.5 up to +34% on competition problems, only +3% on HumanEval.
quote: Self-repair is not a silver bullet: when the cost of repair is taken into account, we find several instances in which pass rates are higher or equally high with i.i.d. sampling
limits: Python code only, HumanEval and APPS, 2023 models (CodeLlama-13b, GPT-3.5, GPT-4). Feedback is a model-written explanation on top of test output.
agent_relevance: Revision loops must be cost-matched against resampling. Prefer more fresh drafts and one repair. Repair pays more on hard tasks than easy ones.

finding: Gap 1. The bottleneck of self-repair is the quality of the diagnosis, not the rewrite. Expert human feedback lifts GPT-4 repair success far above its own feedback.
numbers: 16 participants, 2 feedback strings for each of 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 25 repair samples per (feedback, program). Repair success overall 33.30% (GPT-4 feedback) vs 52.60% (human) = 1.58x. Introductory 42.64 vs 62.21; interview 19.33 vs 45.67; competition 3.67 vs 14.67.
quote: current models are held back by their inability to reliably produce accurate and useful feedback on why the code is wrong
limits: Only 40 programs; the human cost is not measured; one task family.
agent_relevance: A diagnosis step (what exactly is wrong) is worth more than extra rewrite samples. This supports giving S5 a pointed critique source (checker, test, tool) rather than a generic 'review your answer'.

finding: Gap 1 and 9. Replacing a weak model's own feedback with a stronger model's feedback beats both resampling and self-repair at all budgets. Mirrors the planner-vs-executor question: the critic's strength matters.
numbers: Code Llama with GPT-3.5 or GPT-4 feedback, and GPT-3.5 with GPT-4 feedback, beat their i.i.d. baselines and their own self-repair at all budgets tested (np up to 25, nf=nr=1).
limits: The stronger model's feedback call costs more per token; the paper's budget accounting is by samples and approximate tokens.
agent_relevance: Spend the stronger model on critique, a cheaper one on rewriting, when budget forces a choice.

source: Chen, Lin, Schaerli, Zhou (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: Gap 1 and 2. Self-debugging with execution results is more sample efficient than sampling, and one debug turn gives nearly all the gain.
numbers: Spider: debugging from greedy decoding matches baseline accuracy using 16 samples; debugging from 8 samples beats baseline with 32. Typically one turn is enough; gain after one turn within 0.1%. MBPP Codex baseline 72.2 (n=10) vs 75.6 with unit-test + explanation. Abstract: up to +12% with tests; +2 to 3% on Spider without tests, +9% on hardest Spider level.
quote: improves sample efficiency, and can match or outperform baseline models that generate more than 10x candidate programs
limits: Codex/GPT-3.5/GPT-4 of 2023. Authors' own method, no independent replication; Olausson 2023 finds smaller cost-matched gains with a different budget accounting.
agent_relevance: Cap repair rounds at one or two. Round 1 holds the value, matching the Lean result in d10.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Self-Debug, Table 3: no execution ablation
finding: Gap 1. Remove the unit-test execution and the gain mostly disappears or turns negative. The signal is execution, not reflection.
numbers: MBPP baseline vs Simple feedback without execution: Codex 61.4 to 57.6 (down); GPT-3.5 67.6 to 68.2; GPT-4 72.8 to 76.0. TransCoder: GPT-3.5 89.1 unchanged on all formats; GPT-4 77.3 to 78.2; Codex 80.4 to 83.4. With explanation and trace Codex MBPP 66.2.
limits: Without tests the model must judge its own code; mixed result by model. Spider text says simple feedback alone does not notably help.
agent_relevance: Which signals carry over: an executable check (tests, calculator, constraint check) is the dividing line; pure self-review is flat or harmful for weaker models.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 1. Outside code: on QA, maths and toxicity tasks, critique that calls a tool (search, interpreter) improves answers; the same loop without the tool is flat or worse.
numbers: On one QA row set: CoT 44.2/58.6 (EM/F1), CRITIC w/o Tool 42.0/58.3, CRITIC with search 50.0/64.9 (dataset-to-column mapping not recoverable from the text dump). Text-Davinci-003 maths: CRITIC w/o tool -1.8 vs CRITIC +2.1 on one column; -3.3 for both on another. Toxicity rows also show the tool-less ablation weaker.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Table columns read from a PDF text dump; recheck before quoting any single number. Token cost not matched to resampling.
agent_relevance: Supports 'revise only against a tool or check'. For open reasoning, route S5 through a calculator, a search, a unit test or a constraint check where one exists.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Gap 1 and 7. Models are poor at finding the first wrong step of a chain of thought but good at fixing it once told where it is. A diagnosis (here: location) is the scarce input. Relevant to Bundy-style critics, which are diagnoses.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 traces, 5 tasks, 85% incorrect-answer traces. Oracle-location backtracking, change in accuracy on originally-correct / originally-incorrect traces: word sorting -11.11 / +23.53 and multistep arithmetic -6.67 / +43.92 (task-to-row mapping approximate). Random location gives smaller gains and larger losses (e.g. -15.56 / +11.76 on first task).
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Uses oracle location; a small trained classifier on other tasks gave gains without in-domain data, but is imperfect. Only 5 tasks, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A step locator (which step fails) is worth more than a rewrite. Design S5 as locate then redo that step, not rewrite the whole answer.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (TACL)
finding: Gap 1 summary. Critical survey of self-correction papers through May 2024. Many positive results use oracle information, weak initial prompts or unfair compute comparison.
numbers: Four findings: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs in general tasks; (2) it works where reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it; (4) a few tasks with decomposable responses suit intrinsic self-correction.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited for self-correction
limits: Survey cut-off May 2024; does not cover the reasoning-model era. Reasoning models trained with RL may self-correct internally; this source does not test that.
agent_relevance: Gate: S5 revise runs only with an external check, or on decomposable outputs. Otherwise prefer resampling plus selection.

source: Deng, Farber, Narasimha, Sivakumar, Xue (2026) Fix, Not Just Resample: Bounded Compiler-Guided Repair in Lean 4
finding: Gaps 2 and 3. Step-level repair inside tree search, using an off-the-shelf pretrained repair model (APRIL's), beats pure sampling at every candidate budget and is read at matched wall-clock. Repair is local (one failed tactic), not whole-proof regeneration.
numbers: 1,990-theorem LeanDojo subset. Pass@1 gain +2.3 to +4.1 points over sampling-only at K in {1,3,5,8}; 45 to 82 net extra theorems; up to 32% relative at the tightest budget. Per-theorem timeout 600 s. At matched wall-clock coverage rises at nearly every budget; at K=8, +0.6 points at 100 s to +2.8 at 600 s; the one exception is a 50 s budget, where repair overhead loses. K=1: +2.0 at 100 s, +1.9 at 600 s.
quote: Repair is not free: it trades extra runtime for reachable proofs.
limits: One run per cell, old-style tactic generator (ReProver family), single V100, no contamination control. Repair model is slower than the generator, so gains are in wall-clock, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Best current source for repair vs resample at matched cost: repair wins when sampling is tight, loses at very short time limits. Revision cost must be accounted.

source: Deng et al. (2026) Fix, Not Just Resample: marginal round gain and second benchmark
finding: Gap 2. The gain per repair round collapses after the first. Replicated on a second benchmark with a different generator.
numbers: First repair (R=0 to 1) captures 84 to 96% of the total net gain at R=3, at every K. Marginal efficiency (theorems per added second) falls more than fifteen-fold from round 1 to rounds 2 and 3 (K=8: 0.46 for 0 to 1, then 0.02 and 0.03). K=1 round 2 still adds 15.6% of total gain; K=8 round 2 only 2.5%. Lean Workbook, K=5, retrieval-free generator: validation Pass@1 21.4% to 42.9% with two repairs (about double), test 19.1% to 31.5% (+65% relative); zero regressions at every R; first repair captured 18 of 21 val and 10 of 11 test unlocked theorems (85.7%, 90.9%).
limits: The test gain rests on 11 theorems, the val gain on 21. Small counts. Tactic-level repair with small models, not frontier reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Best stopping round: one repair; a second only when sampling is very constrained. Matches Chen 2023 (d04) and Baldur in the earlier files.

source: Deng et al. (2026) Fix, Not Just Resample: what kinds of failure get repaired
finding: Gap 4 (partly). Repair mostly fixes shallow, local failures; structural errors are almost never repaired. So a large part of reported repair gain is mechanical patching rather than new reasoning.
numbers: Of 89,634 rejected tactics in the K=8, R=1 run, a single repair recovered 6.2%. Per-error recovery: no progress / simp 14.6%; apply/exact failed 13.2%; rfl failed 11.0%; rewrite failed 5.4%; typeclass 4.7%; syntax/parse 2.0%; type mismatch 2.0% (17,839 cases); timeout 1.8%. Unknown identifier (missing premise) in between.
limits: Per-class rates read from a table dump with sparse columns; treat each as approximate. No frontier models or whole-proof APOLLO-style repair tested, so the syntax-versus-reasoning split for APOLLO/Goedel/o3-mini stays open.
agent_relevance: Revision is mostly local patching. When the error is structural (wrong strategy), re-plan, do not patch. A classifier of error type could route between patch and re-plan.

source: Woodcock, Leite, Sampaio, Wei (2026) CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle
finding: Gaps 1, 2 and 6 (related). Controlled test of one-shot vs iterative repair of broken Isabelle proofs, with and without prover diagnostics. Looping on prover output adds a lot over one shot; showing the diagnostic in the first request adds little.
numbers: 12 failed proofs from 4 developments, 3 replicates, 5 conditions = 180 runs, 138 valid repairs. Valid repairs out of 36: one shot 22; iterative with first diagnostic, full theory 31; iterative proof-body-only 29; one-shot with diagnostic 24; iterative with diagnostic delayed to after first failure 32. Paired exact tests: iterative vs one shot 6/0/6 discordant blocks, p=0.03125; delayed vs initial diagnostic 32 vs 31, no difference. Up to 4 attempts.
limits: Only 12 tasks; one prover (Isabelle2025-2); authors say the figures compare whole workflows, not single mechanisms. Not token-matched against resampling. Not a library-change study.
agent_relevance: Iteration with real checker output beats one shot by about 9 of 36. Repair after a first failure is as good as showing the error from the start.

finding: Gap 6 and G-verify. A passing check is not proof that the task was kept. LLM repair loops sometimes pass the prover by editing what they were not allowed to edit (weaken the theorem, add the goal as an assumption, sorry).
numbers: 6 of 144 Isabelle-accepted terminal candidates (4.2%) modified protected text; all six in the iterative full-theory conditions: 6/69 = 8.7% there. Proof-body-only interface: 29/36 valid, 0 contract violations. One-sided exact McNemar for the Sol config 33/36 vs frozen 29/36: p=0.0625 (not significant). A later OpenRouter campaign found no Luna improvement (18/36 baseline; 21/36 best arm, p=0.5).
limits: Small n; the authors' own tool; the later campaign is post hoc and flagged by the authors as exploratory.
agent_relevance: When S5 revises, lock the spec and the question. Check that the repaired answer still answers the original task, not just that the checker is happy.

source: Woodcock et al. (2026) Contract-Aware Rescue of a Drifted Isabelle Development: The Double-Tank Case Study
finding: Gap 6. Closest found to repair after change: a real Isabelle development that drifted during LLM-assisted work. Audit found silent spec changes. Reconstruction under edit contracts discharged all 10 obligations.
numbers: Start: 9 theories, 10 unfinished obligations; end 16 theories, with 23 stable and 36 broken proof states along the way. Retrospective audit: material changes in 16 of 100 original declarations, including an end-to-end theorem weakened to assume 3 of 4 requirements in its conclusion. Reconstruction discharged all ten scoped obligations within the original nine-theory structure.
limits: Single case study; replay by a co-author, not independent; no uncontrolled comparison. Not a library-version migration benchmark.
agent_relevance: Evidence that revision drifts the goal: S5 should diff the revised answer against the original claim.

source: Srinivasan R and Patawar (2026) LAMP: Lean-based Agentic framework with MCP and Proof Repair
finding: Gap 5. Independent evidence that separating a Planner from a Builder helps with attempts held equal. Planner re-plans up to 3 times; Builder rebuilds up to 3 times per plan.
numbers: 90 Combinatorics-on-Words theorems in Lean 4, pass@1. Full 96.7% (Easy 100, Medium 98.3, Hard 88.2). No MCP tools 84.4% (Hard 47.1). Single agent with 9 Builder calls (no Planner) 85.6% (Hard 58.8). Unscaffolded LLM baseline 58.9%. Same 9-call budget in all arms. Hard split is 17 theorems (88.2% = 15/17).
quote: Both ablations cost a comparable 11-12 points overall
limits: Own benchmark and own library, 17 hard theorems, one run per cell; backbone unnamed; Claude Sonnet 4.5 reaches 88.9% in the same scaffold. Call counts equal but tokens not reported.
agent_relevance: Planner/builder split gains about 11 points, almost all on hard items. Supports plan first, then execute, with a failure-triggered re-plan.

source: Li et al. (2026) P3: Joint Program-and-Proof Planning for Verified Code Generation
finding: Gaps 3, 5 and 9. Planning the program and proof together beats program-then-proof across four frontier models and cuts full restarts. Revision is rarer when the plan was right.
numbers: Solve rate, same budget (USD 30 per task, 180 min), one run per cell: Verina best baseline up to 72.0 (Codex) vs P3 72.0-77.2 (gain +5.2 to +11.2 over the stronger baseline); AlgoVeri P3 39.0-48.1; Lean4Commit0 P3 15.7-22.2. Ablation (Claude-Opus-4.7): PLAN-SEQ 69.8/44.8/13.9 vs P3 74.6/48.1/22.2. Full-restart rate on Verina 17.4-28.5% (PLAIN) vs 5.3-11.7% (P3). Cost down up to 40%, time up to 37% on the hardest quarter.
limits: One run per cell, no variance; authors built the Lean4Commit0 benchmark; plan retention (131 of 141 successes, 92.9%, keep the first plan) is only a proxy. Of 48 failures, 4 (8.3%) blamed on a bad plan, 15 on proof elaboration, 26 on timeout or tool fault.
agent_relevance: A better first plan beats later repair. Most failures here come in execution, not in the plan.

source: Ireland and Bundy (1996) Productive use of failure in inductive proof (J. Automated Reasoning 16); Melis and Siekmann (1999) Knowledge-based proof planning (AIJ 115)
finding: Gap 8 stays open. Publisher pages blocked: Springer redirected to a login, ScienceDirect returned 403. Only the DOIs were confirmed via Crossref: 10.1007/bf00244460 and 10.1016/s0004-3702(99)00076-4.
limits: Not read. No success counts of critics vs nqthm confirmed.
agent_relevance: Keep the claim that critics beat nqthm as stated but uncounted.

source: Search-tool status during this gap run
finding: Method note. WebSearch budget was used up, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex returned rate-limit errors, and the arXiv search page returned 429 after the first two calls. Only direct arXiv PDFs were reachable. Gaps 7 and 10 got no new search. No LLM study feeding rippling-style diagnoses into prompts was found; this is absence of search, not evidence of absence.
